content: Acoustics is a multidisciplinary scientific field that focuses on the study of sound, including ultrasound and infrasound, which are mechanical waves propagating through gases, liquids, and solids. Professionals who specialize in this field are known as acousticians, while the practical application of acoustics in technology is referred to as acoustical engineering. There is significant overlap and collaboration between the work of acousticians and acoustical engineers. Hearing is a vital survival mechanism in the animal kingdom, and speech is a defining feature of human development and culture. Consequently, the science of acoustics permeates numerous aspects of society, including music, medicine, architecture, industrial production, and even warfare. The interplay of art, craftsmanship, science, and technology has driven advancements in the field, as in many other areas of knowledge. The term acoustic originates from the ancient Greek word ἀκουστός (akoustos), meaning able to be heard, while its Latin equivalent is sonic. As acousticians expanded their research to include frequencies beyond the audible range, these were categorized as ultrasonic (above the audible range) and infrasonic (below the audible range). The term acoustic now encompasses the entire frequency spectrum without limitation. History of Acoustics Early Research in Acoustics The origins of acoustics as a science can be traced back to Greek and Roman cultures between the 6th century BCE and the 1st century BCE. Initially, the study of acoustics was closely tied to music, which had been practiced as an art form for millennia. However, it was not until Pythagoras began investigating the nature of musical intervals that a scientific approach emerged. Pythagoras sought to understand why certain intervals were perceived as more harmonious and discovered that these could be explained through numerical ratios. Around 20 BCE, the Roman architect and engineer Vitruvius wrote a treatise on the acoustical properties of theaters, addressing phenomena such as interference, echoes, and reverberation. This work marked the beginnings of architectural acoustics. The physical understanding of acoustical processes advanced significantly during and after the Scientific Revolution. Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) and Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) independently formulated the complete laws governing vibrating strings, building upon the work initiated by Pythagoras two millennia earlier. Galileo notably described sound waves as vibrations of a sonorous body that propagate through the air, stimulating the tympanum of the ear and being interpreted by the mind as sound. This insight laid the foundation for physiological and psychological acoustics. Experimental measurements of the speed of sound in air were successfully conducted between 1630 and 1680 by various researchers, including Mersenne. Meanwhile, Isaac Newton (1642–1727) derived the relationship for wave velocity in solids, a cornerstone of physical acoustics, as presented in his seminal work Principia (1687). The Age of Enlightenment and Beyond The 18th century witnessed significant progress in acoustics, driven by the application of calculus to wave propagation theory by prominent mathematicians of the era. In the 19th century, Helmholtz in Germany consolidated the field of physiological acoustics, while Lord Rayleigh in England synthesized existing knowledge and contributed extensively to the field in his monumental work The Theory of Sound. Additionally, Wheatstone, Ohm, and Henry developed analogies between electricity and acoustics. The 20th century saw a proliferation of technological applications of acoustical science. Sabine's pioneering work in architectural acoustics was among the first, followed by advancements in underwater acoustics for submarine detection during World War I. Innovations in sound recording and telecommunication transformed global society. The use of electronics and computing enabled unprecedented accuracy and sophistication in sound measurement and analysis. The ultrasonic frequency range facilitated novel applications in medicine and industry, such as ultrasonography and elastography. New types of transducers, which generate and receive acoustic energy, were invented and widely utilized. Fundamental Concepts of Acoustics The study of acoustics revolves around the generation, propagation, and reception of mechanical waves and vibrations. These processes involve various natural and volitional causes, as well as transduction mechanisms that convert energy from one form into acoustic energy, producing sound waves. A fundamental equation governs acoustic wave propagation, but the resulting phenomena are diverse and often complex. Acoustic waves carry energy through the medium in which they propagate, eventually being transduced into other forms of energy. The final effects may be purely physical or extend into biological or volitional domains. The five basic steps of an acoustical process—generation, propagation, reception, transduction, and effect—are universally applicable, whether describing an earthquake, a submarine using sonar, or a rock concert. The central aspect of acoustics is wave propagation, which falls under the domain of physical acoustics. In fluids, sound propagates primarily as pressure waves, while in solids, mechanical waves can take various forms, including longitudinal, transverse, and surface waves. Acoustics examines pressure levels and frequencies in sound waves, with transduction processes being of particular importance. Wave Propagation: Pressure Levels In fluids such as air and water, sound waves propagate as disturbances in ambient pressure levels. Although these disturbances are typically small, they are perceptible to the human ear. The faintest sound detectable by humans, known as the threshold of hearing, is nine orders of magnitude smaller than ambient pressure. The loudness of these disturbances is quantified as the sound pressure level (SPL), measured on a logarithmic scale in decibels (dB). Mathematically, SPL is defined as: [ text{SPL} = 20 cdot log_{10} left( frac{P}{P_{text{ref}}} right) ] where ( P_{text{ref}} ) is the threshold of hearing and ( P ) is the change in pressure from the ambient level. Wave Propagation: Frequency Physicists and acoustical engineers often discuss sound pressure levels in terms of frequency, as this aligns with how the human ear perceives sound. Higher-pitched sounds correspond to higher frequencies, while lower-pitched sounds correspond to lower frequencies. Acoustic signals are often sampled over time and presented in formats such as octave bands or time-frequency plots to facilitate analysis and understanding. The frequency spectrum is divided into three sections: audio (20 Hz to 20,000 Hz), ultrasonic (above 20,000 Hz), and infrasonic (below 20 Hz). The audio range is significant for human hearing and has applications in speech and music. The ultrasonic range, with its shorter wavelengths, is used in medical imaging technologies like ultrasonography. The infrasonic range is employed in studying geological phenomena such as earthquakes. Transduction in Acoustics A transducer is a device that converts one form of energy into another. In acoustics, this typically involves converting sound energy into electrical energy or vice versa. Acoustic transducers are essential for nearly all applications in the field and include devices such as loudspeakers, microphones, hydrophones, sonar projectors, and ultrasound imaging equipment. Most of these are electromechanical devices that convert electrical signals to or from sound pressure waves. For example, subwoofers generate low-frequency sound waves using a suspended diaphragm that oscillates to produce pressure waves. Similarly, electret microphones operate by converting sound waves striking their surface into electrical signals. Divisions of Acoustics As our understanding of the physics underlying acoustics has advanced, numerous subfields have emerged. The PACS classification system identifies 17 major subfields of acoustics, which are grouped into three domains: physical acoustics, biological acoustics, and acoustical engineering.
